checkpoints.prompt: Which is an appropriate purpose of running the same build and tests for every small commit?

choices.text: Shorten the gap between a change and a failure, making it easier to pinpoint what needs fixing
choices.explanation: Frequent automated checks keep the changes at each integration point small and make it easier to trace the cause.

choices.text: Hide failures until the next release
choices.explanation: CI is a mechanism for detecting failures early.

choices.text: Skip tests to make builds faster
choices.explanation: CI aims to check integration quality early; it is not about skipping checks.

choices.text: Combine commits and run a single manual check
choices.explanation: Checking a large set of changes later makes it harder to identify the cause of a failure.

checkpoints.title: CI: Check Small Commits

checkpoints.prompt: What describes a state in which an artifact can be deployed at any time after approval, without being deployed to production automatically?

choices.text: continuous delivery
choices.explanation: Delivery puts validated changes in a deployable state, while execution of deployment can be separated by an approval gate.

choices.text: continuous deployment only
choices.explanation: Deployment means putting changes into a live environment; it is distinct from automatic deployment without approval.

choices.text: source control commit
choices.explanation: A commit records a change; it is not itself the state of having a deployable artifact.

choices.text: rollback
choices.explanation: Rollback is the act of returning to a previous version; it is not a delivery state.

checkpoints.title: Separating delivery from deployment

checkpoints.prompt: Which method is appropriate for proving that the same artifact was used in both the test and production environments?

choices.text: Record the build artifact’s digest and verify that it matches in both environments.
choices.explanation: A digest provides a basis for identifying the same artifact across environments.

choices.text: Rebuild from the source separately for each environment and give the builds the same name.
choices.explanation: Even with the same name, separate builds may have different contents.

choices.text: Match only the deployment times.
choices.explanation: Deployment times do not show that the artifact contents are identical.

choices.text: Resolve dependencies again in production.
choices.explanation: Regenerating artifacts separately for each environment breaks the principle of promoting the same artifact.

checkpoints.title: Build an artifact once and promote it

checkpoints.prompt: When an integration test fails in a pipeline, choose two decisions that safely stop promotion.

choices.text: Treat the failure as a failed gate and stop subsequent stages.
choices.explanation: A quality gate prevents a failed change from advancing to the next stage.

choices.text: Record the cause of failure and the conditions for rerunning, then retest after making the fix.
choices.explanation: Keeping a record through reproduction, fixing, and retesting provides evidence, not just a stop.

choices.text: Ignore the failed stage and proceed to production.
choices.explanation: Ignoring the gate means test results no longer serve as a condition for promotion.

choices.text: Delete the test results and treat the run as successful.
choices.explanation: Deleting the results destroys quality evidence and only hides the failure.

checkpoints.title: Stop at the gate and promote in stages

choices.text: Source is where changes enter the pipeline.
choices.explanation: The source stage incorporates changes.

choices.text: Test detects issues early.
choices.explanation: The test stage checks quality before deployment.

choices.text: Deploy always sends changes to production, regardless of the test results.
choices.explanation: The pipeline should be designed so that quality gates or approvals can stop deployment.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about CI/CD.
finalQuestions.title: Pipeline

choices.text: Run automated tests before production deployment.
choices.explanation: This is a gate that checks changes early.

choices.text: Continue deployment even when the build fails.
choices.explanation: A failed result stops deployment.

choices.text: Do not keep a known-good version for rollback.
choices.explanation: You need to preserve the ability to recover.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the two statements that are incorrect about safe CI/CD operations.
finalQuestions.title: Safe releases

choices.text: Check the conditions for proceeding to the next stage, and stop progress if they are not met.
choices.explanation: A gate is a checkpoint that verifies success criteria; later stages cannot proceed until those criteria are met.

choices.text: If a check fails, skip it and proceed to the next stage.
choices.explanation: Lowering the criteria to let the process pass goes against a gate’s role of verifying quality.

choices.text: When the scheduled time arrives, start deployment regardless of the check results.
choices.explanation: A scheduled time is no substitute for quality criteria. If they are not met, stop progress.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct description of the role of a quality gate.
finalQuestions.title: CI starting point

choices.text: Narrow down the cause using logs.
choices.explanation: Logs provide clues for investigating the cause.

choices.text: Rerun the same check after fixing the issue.
choices.explanation: Confirm the result of the fix.

choices.text: Proceed to deploy even if the check fails.
choices.explanation: A failed check stops subsequent stages.

finalQuestions.prompt: When CI fails, select one incorrect response.
finalQuestions.title: When CI Fails

choices.text: It is easier to detect defects while changes are still small.
choices.explanation: Frequent integration helps narrow down the cause.

choices.text: A successful CI run guarantees there will be no production incidents.
choices.explanation: CI does not guarantee everything.

choices.text: Build and test results can inform the next decision.
choices.explanation: Test results can be used to decide whether to promote.

choices.text: You can integrate while hiding failures.
choices.explanation: Failures should be recorded and fixed.

choices.text: Approvals and monitoring are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: CI alone does not eliminate the need for operational decisions.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct benefits of CI.
finalQuestions.title: Benefits of CI

choices.text: Delivery always deploys to production without approval.
choices.explanation: Delivery means the software is ready to be deployed.

choices.text: Deployment automates the process through to production deployment after checks.
choices.explanation: Continuous deployment proceeds all the way to production deployment.

choices.text: Deployment does not check the artifact.
choices.explanation: A gate is necessary even for automated deployment.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about delivery and deployment.
finalQuestions.title: Delivery and deployment

choices.text: Keep the inspected version as a candidate.
choices.explanation: This lets you identify the item awaiting approval.

choices.text: Review the change impact and monitoring plan.
choices.explanation: Approval is an operational control point.

choices.text: Skip inspection because the approver replaces the test.
choices.explanation: Approval does not replace automated checks.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the one incorrect statement about a procedure that includes approval.
finalQuestions.title: The Role of Approval

choices.text: Delivery keeps software ready for production release.
choices.explanation: The core of delivery is keeping software in a releasable state.

choices.text: Deployment always requires manual approval.
choices.explanation: Continuous deployment can also happen without approval.

choices.text: Adding an approval means tests are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: Approval is not a substitute for testing.

choices.text: Approval lets you review the impact and monitoring plan.
choices.explanation: It is a checkpoint for assessing operational risk.

choices.text: Delivery rebuilds the artifact every time.
choices.explanation: Artifact identity is a separate design concern.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct statements about delivery, deployment, and approvals.
finalQuestions.title: Delivery models

choices.text: Inspect an artifact built once, then promote that same artifact across environments.
choices.explanation: This reduces differences between the artifact that was validated and the one used in production.

choices.text: Build a separate artifact for each environment.
choices.explanation: Rebuilding can produce differences in the contents.

choices.text: Do not record the version or digest.
choices.explanation: This is necessary to track artifact identity.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the two statements that are incorrect about artifact promotion.
finalQuestions.title: Same artifact

choices.text: Check the digest verified in staging.
choices.explanation: This lets you confirm that it is the same artifact.

choices.text: Deploy a different artifact rebuilt for production.
choices.explanation: Avoid this because it creates a difference from the artifact that was verified.

choices.text: Skip identifying the artifact to be deployed because configuration can be injected externally.
choices.explanation: Separating configuration and confirming artifact identity are separate checks. Track by version or digest whether the executable being deployed is the same one that was verified.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct procedure for promoting from staging to production.
finalQuestions.title: Rebuild

choices.text: Save the version or digest.
choices.explanation: This lets you identify the artifact being distributed.

choices.text: Rewrite the files for each environment.
choices.explanation: This breaks the artifact’s identity.

choices.text: Associate the originating commit with the inspection results.
choices.explanation: This lets you track provenance.

choices.text: Delete the inspected artifact and rebuild it.
choices.explanation: You can’t promote the same artifact this way.

choices.text: Treat artifacts as identical even when their digests differ.
choices.explanation: Different digests mean different artifacts.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two correct ways to track artifacts securely.
finalQuestions.title: Artifact Tracking

choices.text: Promote to production after checking the baseline in staging.
choices.explanation: Check quality at each stage.

choices.text: Proceed at the scheduled time even if the gate fails.
choices.explanation: Stop if the conditions are not met.

choices.text: Define who is responsible and how to rerun after a failure.
choices.explanation: Make the gate an effective stopping point.

choices.text: Lower the threshold to pass if failures continue.
choices.explanation: Resolve the cause without lowering the quality requirements.

choices.text: Ensure the previous healthy version can be maintained.
choices.explanation: This limits the impact of a failure.
